passage: I'm Kashish, and I sit next to Shreya. Today two boys kept talking during the test, so Ma'am said the whole class would lose recess. Everyone groaned. Shreya put her hand up. Her voice shook a bit, but she said, "Ma'am, is it fair to punish everyone for what two people did?" The room went silent. Ma'am thought for a moment. "Maybe not. The two talkers will stay in. The rest can go." I wasn't sure if Shreya was scared or just brave. Maybe both.

qa.q: Why did Ma'am say the whole class would lose recess?
qa.a: Because two boys kept talking during the test.

qa.q: What does Shreya's shaking voice suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt nervous about speaking up to the teacher.

qa.q: What could students learn from how Shreya raised her concern?
qa.a: They can question a rule politely with a clear reason instead of complaining.

qa.q: How might Ma'am see Shreya's question?
qa.a: She seems to take it seriously and agree the punishment was unfair to the rest.

grounding: A classmate observes a child questioning whether a group punishment is fair.

passage:
Week one: The school's new rule said anyone late to assembly would miss games period. On Monday the bus broke down and Minakshi missed games. "It wasn't my fault!" she told Rafiq, her father, at dinner. "Is it fair?" he asked. "Not for bus kids."
Week two: Minakshi and three others wrote a letter to the principal explaining that late buses weren't their choice. Rafiq helped with spelling but not ideas.
Week three: The principal changed the rule: bus delays wouldn't count. Minakshi ran to games period grinning.

qa.q: What broke down on Monday?
qa.a: The bus broke down.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's "It wasn't my fault!" show about her feelings?
qa.a: It shows she felt the punishment was unfair and frustrating.

qa.q: What went right in how Minakshi challenged the rule?
qa.a: She and others wrote a clear, polite letter explaining why the rule was unfair to bus children.

qa.q: How might other bus children be affected by the rule change?
qa.a: They won't be punished for delays they can't control, which feels fairer.

grounding: It shows a child judging a rule's fairness and working to make it proportionate over weeks.

passage: "Zainab, you think your team's rule is unfair? Let me tell you about my hockey days. Our coach once benched the whole team for a match because one girl came late. We lost badly. Afterwards I asked him, 'Should eleven people pay for one person's mistake?' He was quiet. The next season he made new rules: the late person runs extra laps, not the whole team. Nobody complained. Fairness means the consequence fits the mistake and the person." Aditi Phuphi sipped her tea. "Now, what's happening in your team?"

qa.q: Why did Aditi's coach bench the whole team?
qa.a: Because one girl came late.

qa.q: What might Aditi have been feeling when she asked the coach her question?
qa.a: She likely felt the punishment was unfair and was frustrated by losing.

qa.q: What lesson does Aditi share about fair consequences?
qa.a: That a consequence should fit the mistake and fall on the person who made it.

qa.q: How might the late girl have felt about the whole team being benched?
qa.a: She probably felt guilty that everyone paid for her mistake.

grounding: An elder tells a story of debating whether a team punishment was proportionate and fair.

passage: The school bus left in ten minutes, and class six was still sitting in silence. Someone had drawn a moustache on the principal's photo, and nobody owned up, so Mrs Rao had cancelled sports day practice for all of them. Siddharth, eleven, raised his hand. 'Ma'am, can I say something quickly?' She nodded. 'The drawing was wrong. But forty kids losing practice for one person's joke feels too big. And some of us weren't even in the room.' Pradeep whispered, 'You'll get us in more trouble.' Mrs Rao tapped her pen. 'What would be fair, then?' 'Only those who were here stay back and clean it. Everyone else practises.' She thought, then agreed.

qa.q: Why had Mrs Rao cancelled sports day practice?
qa.a: Someone drew a moustache on the principal's photo and nobody owned up.

qa.q: What was Pradeep worried about when Siddharth spoke up?
qa.a: Pradeep feared that questioning the teacher would make things worse for the whole class.

qa.q: What made Siddharth's argument persuasive?
qa.a: He admitted the drawing was wrong, explained why the punishment was too big, and offered a fairer alternative.

qa.q: How might the children who weren't in the room see the new decision?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and that they had been treated fairly at last.

grounding: Shows a child debating whether a group punishment is proportionate and fair to all, under time pressure.

passage: In their Jaipur colony, the cricket rule was clear: hit the ball into Mrs Kulkarni's garden and you were banned for a week. On Sunday, Anand, nine, swung hard and the ball sailed over her hedge. He knew the rule, but his stomach dropped. 'A whole week? It was an accident!' Disha, his twelve-year-old sister, was captain. 'Rules are rules.' 'But when Bunty hit it there on purpose last month, he also got one week. That's the same for doing it on purpose and by mistake.' Disha frowned. Other kids gathered. 'Okay,' she said slowly, 'so maybe first accident is just out. On purpose, one week.' Everyone voted. Anand fetched the ball and said sorry to Mrs Kulkarni.

qa.q: What was the colony rule about Mrs Kulkarni's garden?
qa.a: Anyone who hit the ball into her garden was banned for a week.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when the ball went over the hedge?
qa.a: He felt a sinking dread, since he knew the rule, and then it seemed unfair because it was an accident.

qa.q: What made Anand's point about Bunty a strong one?
qa.a: He showed the same punishment was given for an accident and a deliberate act, which isn't proportionate.

qa.q: Why might Disha have changed her mind as captain?
qa.a: She saw that treating an accident like a deliberate hit wasn't fair to everyone, and a vote kept the group together.

grounding: Shows children debating whether a punishment is proportionate and revising a rule fairly.
